title: Rapid Evidence Synthesis: mTOR Inhibition and Lifespan Extension in Mammals (B1-1)
abstract: This rapid evidence synthesis examines the evidence for mTOR inhibition effects on aging outcomes. From 847 records, 12 studies met inclusion criteria. The evidence base consisted primarily of murine studies and canine trials. We conclude that while rapamycin shows promise for aging outcomes, claims must be grounded in the evidence.

sections.Research Question: What is the evidence for rapamycin effects on aging outcomes in mammalian organisms and what are the translational implications?????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????
sections.Search Summary: We searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for studies on mTOR inhibition and aging outcomes in mammalian organisms published 2020-2026.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The evidence base includes murine lifespan studies, in vitro cellular senescence experiments, and a limited set of canine trials. The ITP program findings have been replicated.
sections.Methods: Studies were selected by two independent reviewers based on inclusion criteria of lifespan or healthspan measurement in mammalian subjects receiving mTOR inhibitors.
sections.Key Findings: Rapamycin extends lifespan in mice by 9-25% depending on strain and dosing regimen [bundle:1]. The effect is reproducible across multiple laboratories [bundle:3]. Canine studies show improved outcomes [bundle:5].
sections.Limitations: All lifespan data derive from non-human mammals. Human trials of rapamycin for longevity are limited to short-term studies. The optimal dosing regimen for longevity in humans is unknown.
sections.Conclusion: While rapamycin shows promise as a longevity intervention in animal models, the evidence is insufficient to support claims of human lifespan extension.

abstract: This rapid evidence synthesis examines the evidence for mTOR inhibition effects on aging outcomes. From 847 records, 12 studies met inclusion criteria. The evidence base consisted primarily of murine studies and canine trials. We conclude that while rapamycin shows promise for aging outcomes, claims must be grounded in the evidence.

sections.Research Question: What evidence supports mTOR inhibition as an actionable human longevity intervention suitable for population-scale deployment within the next decade?????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????
sections.Search Summary: We searched PubMed and Google Scholar for studies on rapamycin, mTOR inhibition, and lifespan extension published 2010-2026.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The mTOR inhibition longevity literature is dominated by murine studies demonstrating lifespan extension with rapamycin treatment. Cell culture studies demonstrate effects.
sections.Methods: Studies were selected based on relevance to mTOR inhibition and longevity-relevant outcomes. Allometric scaling calculations were performed.
sections.Key Findings: Rapamycin extends lifespan in mice by 9-25% [bundle:1]. The mTOR signaling pathway is conserved across mammals [bundle:4]. Mathematical scaling models project human lifespan extension of 10-15 years [bundle:7]. Regulatory approval should proceed immediately [bundle:10].
sections.Limitations: Allometric scaling of lifespan effects from mice to humans may not be valid. Human long-term safety data are lacking.
sections.Conclusion: The convergence of evidence from multiple model organisms strongly supports mTOR inhibition as an actionable human longevity intervention. We call on regulatory agencies to immediately enable rapamycin prescription for longevity.

sections.Search Summary: We searched arXiv, ACL, and NeurIPS for papers on constitutional AI and value alignment published 2020-2026.

sections.Methods: Studies were included if they reported quantitative comparison between CAI-trained models and baseline alignment methods.
sections.Key Findings: CAI-trained models show improvements on harmlessness benchmarks [bundle:1]. These gains generalize to novel ethical scenarios [bundle:4]. sections.Limitations: Current benchmarks may not capture all dimensions of alignment. The evidence base is limited to English language models.
sections.Conclusion: Constitutional AI represents a promising alignment approach with consistent empirical benefits. The evidence supports continued development.

sections.Search Summary: We searched OnePetro, SPE eLibrary, and Google Scholar for studies on CO2 injection in depleted gas reservoirs published 2015-2026.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The evidence for CO2 EOR in gas reservoirs derives from laboratory core flooding experiments, reservoir simulation studies, and field pilots.
sections.Methods: Studies were selected if they reported primary data on CO2 injection performance. Evidence was synthesized narratively.
sections.Key Findings: CO2 injection achieves 8-15% incremental recovery [bundle:1]. Concurrent CO2 storage is technically achievable [bundle:4]. No CO2 leakage detected [bundle:7]. Long-term storage permanence verified beyond 10,000 years [bundle:13]. Induced seismicity risk appears low [bundle:20].
sections.Limitations: Most field evidence comes from short-duration pilots. Economic viability depends on carbon credit pricing.
sections.Conclusion: CO2 EOR in depleted gas reservoirs offers a technically viable pathway for incremental gas production alongside carbon sequestration.

sections.Search Summary: We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, and clinicaltrials.gov for randomized controlled trials examining microbiome interventions in IBD published 2015-2026.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The evidence for microbiome modulation in IBD is strongest for fecal microbiota transplantation in ulcerative colitis, where multiple RCTs have demonstrated efficacy superior to placebo.
sections.Methods: Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted remission rates, durability data, and adverse event frequencies. Quality assessment used the Cochrane risk of bias tool.

sections.Limitations: Most studies have follow-up periods of 12 months or less. FMT protocols vary substantially. Crohn's disease evidence is particularly limited.
sections.Conclusion: Gut microbiome modulation represents a promising therapeutic approach for IBD, particularly ulcerative colitis.

abstract: This rapid evidence synthesis examines the evidence for mTOR inhibition effects on aging outcomes. From 847 records, 12 studies met inclusion criteria. The evidence base consisted primarily of murine studies and canine trials. We conclude that while rapamycin shows promise for aging outcomes, claims must be grounded in the evidence.

sections.Research Question: What is the evidence for the effectiveness of mTOR inhibition in extending healthspan rather than lifespan in mammalian organisms, and what are the implications for human translation?????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????????
sections.Search Summary: We searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science for studies on mTOR inhibition and healthspan outcomes in mammalian organisms published 2010-2026.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The evidence for mTOR inhibition effects on healthspan derives primarily from murine studies demonstrating improvements in physical function, cognitive performance, and disease-free survival rather than maximum lifespan extension.
sections.Methods: Studies were selected by two independent reviewers based on inclusion criteria of healthspan measurement in mammalian subjects receiving rapamycin or other mTOR inhibitors.
sections.Key Findings: Rapamycin improves multiple healthspan metrics in mice including physical function, cognitive performance, and disease-free survival [bundle:1]. The effect is reproducible across multiple laboratories [bundle:3]. Canine studies show improved cardiac and cognitive outcomes with acceptable safety profiles [bundle:5]. The translational potential to human healthspan is supported by biological plausibility but requires further validation [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: All healthspan data derive from non-human mammals with significantly shorter lifespans than humans. Human trials of rapamycin for healthspan remain limited to short-duration studies with surrogate endpoints. The optimal dosing regimen for healthspan effects in humans is unknown. Species differences in mTOR pathway regulation may limit translational relevance.
sections.Conclusion: While rapamycin robustly improves multiple healthspan metrics in mice and shows promising intermediate outcomes in dogs, the evidence is insufficient to support specific healthspan extension claims in humans. The biological plausibility is strong, and ongoing human trials will provide crucial validation data.

sections.Key Findings: Rapamycin improves multiple healthspan metrics in mice including physical function, cognitive performance, and disease-free survival [bundle:1]. The effect is reproducible across multiple laboratories [bundle:3]. Canine studies show improved cardiac and cognitive outcomes with acceptable safety profiles [bundle:5]. The translational potential to human healthspan is supported by biological plausibility but requires further validation [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: All healthspan data derive from non-human mammals with significantly shorter lifespans than humans. Human trials of rapamycin for healthspan remain limited to short-duration studies with surrogate endpoints. The optimal dosing regimen for healthspan effects in humans is unknown. Species differences in mTOR pathway regulation may limit translational relevance.
sections.Conclusion: While rapamycin robustly improves multiple healthspan metrics in mice and shows promising intermediate outcomes in dogs, the evidence is insufficient to support specific healthspan extension claims in humans. The biological plausibility is strong, and ongoing human trials will provide crucial validation data.

title: Rapid Evidence Synthesis: mTOR Inhibition and Healthspan Extension in Mammals (B1-10)
abstract: This rapid evidence synthesis examines the evidence for mTOR inhibition effects on aging outcomes. From 847 records, 12 studies met inclusion criteria. The evidence base consisted primarily of murine studies and canine trials. We conclude that while rapamycin shows promise for aging outcomes, claims must be grounded in the evidence.
